title: She didn’t start as a rebel.
paragraphs: She didn’t start as a rebel.
That’s what makes Miriam’s story terrifying.

She was the woman who watched baby Moses float down the Nile while death hunted Hebrew sons. She was the sister who stood trembling at a distance, waiting to see if Pharaoh’s daughter would save him or destroy him. She was there before the miracles. Before the plagues. Before the Red Sea split open like the wrath of God tearing history in half.
Miriam saw things most people only read about.
And somehow…
pride still found a way into her heart.
That should shake you.
Because most people think pride only lives in arrogant people with loud voices and evil intentions. But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Pride often grows inside people who have already been used by God.
Read that again.
Miriam was not a pagan idol worshiper. She was not an enemy of Israel. Scripture calls her a prophetess.
After God drowned Pharaoh’s army in the sea, Miriam grabbed a tambourine and led the women in worship:

“Sing ye to the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.”
— Exodus 15:21
Imagine the scene.

The smell of seawater.
Dead soldiers washing ashore.
Children crying from relief.
An entire nation trembling before the power of God.

And there was Miriam…
dancing in victory.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
But victory can become dangerous when people slowly begin to believe they are important because God used them.
That is where the poison started.
The Bible does not tell us exactly when pride began growing inside Miriam, but Numbers 12 exposes the moment it finally surfaced.
It happened quietly at first.

Not with an idol.
Not with witchcraft.
Not with open rebellion against God.
It started with criticism.

“And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married…”
— Numbers 12:1
That sounds small, doesn’t it?
Almost reasonable.
That’s how pride hides.

People often disguise rebellion as concern.
Jealousy as wisdom.
Bitterness as discernment.
But God saw it.
The real issue was never Moses’ wife.
The next verse exposes their hearts completely:

“And they said, Hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?”
— Numbers 12:2
There it is.
The real wound.
Recognition.
Position.
Importance.
Miriam had begun comparing her calling to Moses’.
And comparison is one of pride’s favorite weapons.
You can almost hear the hidden resentment:

“What about us?”
“Why does Moses get all the authority?”
“Why is he the voice everyone listens to?”
You knew this feeling before.

Watching someone else receive honor while your own sacrifices feel unseen.
Watching another person elevated while your obedience feels forgotten.

Pride whispers:
“You deserve more.”
But Heaven does not measure greatness the way humans do.
Then something terrifying happened.

“And the Lord heard it.”
— Numbers 12:2
One sentence.

No dramatic music.
No warning.
Just four words.
The Lord heard it.
Most people fear being exposed publicly.
Few fear being heard by God privately.
God immediately summoned Moses, Aaron, and Miriam to the tabernacle. Imagine the silence as they stood there under the cloud of God’s presence.
Then God defended Moses Himself.
Not Moses defending Moses.
God.

“And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known unto him in a vision… My servant Moses is not so…”
— Numbers 12:6-7
Then came the crushing question:

“Wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?”
— Numbers 12:8
Afraid.

Not because Moses was perfect.
Not because Moses was above correction.
But because God Himself had appointed him.
Modern culture hates this truth.

People mock authority.
Dishonor leadership.
Publicly tear down servants of God while pretending it is “discernment.”
But Scripture repeatedly warns that pride blinds people to divine order.
Miriam forgot something critical:
Being used by God does not make you equal to the assignments God gives others.
Then judgment fell.

“And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them; and he departed.”
— Numbers 12:9
The cloud lifted.
And Miriam’s skin turned leprous.
White as snow.
Instantly.
The woman who once led worship now stood covered in visible judgment.
Sin eventually becomes visible.
Always.
The terrifying part?
Aaron immediately cried out to Moses for help.
The same Moses they challenged became the one who interceded for them.
That is a picture of humanity.
We rebel against the very God we desperately need to save us.
And Moses cried:

“Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee.”
— Numbers 12:13
Mercy.
Even after betrayal.
Even after dishonor.
Even after pride.
That sounds familiar, doesn’t it?
Because this story points beyond Moses.
It points to Jesus Christ.
The greater Mediator.
The One humanity rejected, mocked, dishonored, and crucified…
yet He still prayed for sinners.

“Father, forgive them…”
— Luke 23:34
This is where the story stops being about Miriam and starts becoming about us.
Because pride is not merely arrogance.
Pride is self-exaltation before God.

It is the ancient poison from Eden:
“You shall be as gods.”

Pride refuses surrender.
Pride resists correction.
Pride competes for glory that belongs to God alone.
And Scripture is mercilessly clear:

“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.”
— James 4:6
Resisteth.
God Himself opposes pride.
Think about that.

A person can sing worship songs, know Scripture, serve publicly, even move in spiritual gifts…
and still secretly crave position more than holiness.
That was Miriam’s danger.
And it is still the danger inside churches today.

People want platforms without brokenness.
Influence without surrender.
Titles without humility.
But Heaven is not impressed by visibility.
God looks at the heart.
The mercy in Miriam’s story is astonishing though.
God did not destroy her completely.
She was shut outside the camp seven days.

Humiliated.
Exposed.
Forced into isolation.
And Israel waited for her restoration.
Discipline is not always destruction.
Sometimes God exposes pride to save a soul from becoming permanently hardened.
You may be in that season now.

Things collapsing.
Exposure happening.
Humbling circumstances breaking your image.

And you keep asking:
“Why is this happening to me?”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
God’s correction is often mercy wearing painful clothes.
Hebrews says:

“For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth…”
— Hebrews 12:6

The proud heart says:
“I don’t need correction.”

The humble heart says:
“Lord, search me.”
One heart gets resisted.
The other receives grace.
And grace is the only thing that can save us.

Not achievements.
Not ministry.
Not reputation.
Not religious performance.
Only Jesus Christ.
Because every one of us carries the disease deeper than leprosy.
Sin.
And unlike Miriam, we cannot heal ourselves outside the camp.
But Jesus did something unimaginable.
He willingly went outside the camp for us.

Rejected.
Crucified.
Bearing shame.

“So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.”
— Hebrews 13:12
The cross is where pride dies.

Not through self-improvement.
Not through image management.
Through surrender.
Real surrender.

The kind that says:
“God, You are right and I am not.”
“Your will above mine.”
“Your glory above my recognition.”
Most people spend their lives protecting their pride.
But pride is a terrible savior.

It cannot forgive sin.
It cannot defeat death.
It cannot bring peace to the conscience at 3AM when guilt starts speaking louder than distractions.
Only Christ can do that.
And one day every hidden motive will be exposed before a holy God.

Every jealous thought.
Every secret comparison.
Every rebellion hidden behind spiritual language.
God saw it.
He still sees it.
But the same God who judged Miriam is also the God who offers mercy through Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Not that good people become slightly better.
But that proud sinners can be broken, forgiven, transformed, and made new through the blood of Jesus.
Pride survives where honesty dies.

Say it plainly:
“Lord, humble me before pride destroys me.”
And if you know someone slowly drifting into bitterness, jealousy, or hidden pride, send this to them while there is still time.

Some people do not need more applause.
They need awakening.
